title: Weird Al Yankovic Now Has an Asteroid Named After Him
summary:
What do you get when you mix a funny singer with outer space? An asteroid named Weird Al! The International Astronomical Union just approved the name Asteroid (14331) Alyankovic for the musician "Weird Al" Yankovic.

Weird Al is famous for funny songs like "Eat It" and "White and Nerdy." He has won five Grammys and even has a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. But this might be his coolest award yet.

The asteroid was discovered in 1981 by Stephen J. Bus in Australia. It is about 1 to 1.25 miles wide — that's like 20 football fields! It orbits the sun between Mars and Jupiter and takes about 1,378 Earth days to go around once.

Why did scientists name an asteroid after a comedian? Dr. Allison McGraw explained that many scientists grew up listening to Weird Al. His songs made learning about science and computers feel fun. "His work has inspired curiosity, creativity, lifelong learning, and a sense of joy in discovering how the world works," she said.

Weird Al had a funny reaction: "I just hope this isn't the asteroid that winds up destroying the Earth."
why_it_matters: It shows that being funny and creative can matter just as much as being serious — the things you love doing now might even get honored by scientists one day.

background_read: The International Astronomical Union is a worldwide group of scientists who give official names to stars, planets and asteroids, and they have named thousands of space objects over the years.
Weird Al Yankovic is a singer and comedian who has spent decades making funny versions of popular songs, so his name is well known to many scientists who grew up listening to him.
The asteroid belt where this asteroid lives sits between Mars and Jupiter and holds millions of rocky leftovers from the time when the solar system was forming.
Article_Structure: WHO: The International Astronomical Union approved the name Asteroid (14331) Alyankovic for musician 'Weird Al' Yankovic, who has five Grammys and a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.
WHAT: The name is now official for an asteroid that was discovered in 1981 by Stephen J. Bus in Australia.
WHERE: The asteroid orbits the sun between Mars and Jupiter, is about 1 to 1.25 miles wide, and takes about 1,378 Earth days to go around once.
WHY: Dr. Allison McGraw said many scientists grew up listening to Weird Al, whose songs made science and computers feel fun and inspired curiosity and lifelong learning.

perspectives.description: They think it is the perfect award for someone whose silly songs made science and computers feel fun for so many people.
They point out that naming asteroids is part of a long tradition of honoring people who inspire curiosity, and that thousands of space objects are already named after famous people.
Some might wonder whether a serious scientific honor should go to a celebrity, or whether the naming is mostly about getting attention.
